pharm: Schizonticidal against asexual erythrocytic forms of Plasmodium; chemically related to quinine.
quick: Treatment: 1250 mg as a single dose; Prophylaxis: 250 mg once weekly
Take with food and at least 240 mL (8 oz) of water; never on an empty stomach
May be used when prophylaxis is needed; weigh risks/benefits
Small amounts excreted in milk; not enough to protect the infant
No adjustment in renal impairment; not removed by dialysis
Half-life may be prolonged; use caution in hepatic impairment
Avoid excessive alcohol; may worsen neuropsychiatric effects
Neuropsychiatric symptoms, cardiac conduction, periodic LFTs and eye exams with long use
summary: Mefloquine is an oral blood schizonticide used to treat mild-to-moderate acute malaria from mefloquine-susceptible P. falciparum (chloroquine-sensitive or -resistant) or P. vivax, and for prophylaxis of P. falciparum and P. vivax malaria. It carries a boxed-style warning: it can cause neuropsychiatric adverse reactions (anxiety, depression, hallucinations, psychosis) that may persist after discontinuation, and it should not be used for prophylaxis in patients with major psychiatric disorders or a history of seizures. P. vivax infections require an 8-aminoquinoline (e.g., primaquine) afterward to prevent relapse.
indications: Treatment of mild to moderate acute malaria caused by mefloquine-susceptible P. falciparum or P. vivax
Prophylaxis of P. falciparum and P. vivax malaria infections

dosage.d: 1250 mg (five 250 mg tablets) as a single dose
dosage.n: Take with food and >=240 mL water; do not retreat if no improvement in 48-72 h

dosage.d: Approximately 20-25 mg/kg as a single dose or split into two doses 6-8 h apart
250 mg once weekly; start 1 week before travel, continue weekly during stay and for 4 weeks after leaving
dosage.n: Take on the same day each week, after the main meal

dosage.d: Weekly weight-based: ~5 mg/kg once weekly (e.g., ~1/4 tab 5-9 kg up to 1 tab >45 kg)
dosage.n: Begin 1-3 weeks before and continue 4 weeks after exposure

admin: Always take with food and a full glass (at least 240 mL) of water; never on an empty stomach
For prophylaxis, take on the same day each week to maintain steady levels
If vomiting occurs within 30-60 minutes of a dose, a repeat (full or half) dose may be needed
After P. vivax, follow with an 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine) to prevent relapse
moa: Mefloquine is a blood schizonticide active against the asexual erythrocytic stages of malaria parasites. Although the exact mechanism is not fully defined, it is structurally related to quinine and is thought to interfere with the parasite's heme detoxification/food-vacuole function, leading to accumulation of toxic heme and parasite death. It does not eliminate the hepatic (exoerythrocytic) stages of P. vivax.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to mefloquine or related compounds (quinine, quinidine) or excipients
For PROPHYLAXIS: active depression or recent history of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, psychosis, schizophrenia or other major psychiatric disorders
relative: Cardiac conduction abnormalities (caution; may prolong QT)
Concurrent use of drugs that prolong QT or lower seizure threshold
monitor: Liver function and ophthalmic exams with prolonged use

preg: Mefloquine may be used for malaria prophylaxis or treatment during pregnancy when the benefit is judged to outweigh the risk; malaria itself poses serious risk to mother and fetus. Weigh risks and benefits and follow current travel-medicine guidance.
lact: Mefloquine is excreted in human milk in small amounts; the quantity is insufficient to protect the infant against malaria. Use with caution.
renal: No dosage adjustment is needed in renal impairment, and mefloquine is not appreciably removed by hemodialysis.
hepatic: In hepatic impairment the elimination of mefloquine may be prolonged, leading to higher plasma levels; use with caution.

major: Drugs that prolong the QT interval (e.g., halofantrine - contraindicated; also quinine, quinidine, chloroquine; antiarrhythmics) - serious arrhythmia risk
Halofantrine (potentially fatal QT prolongation; do not co-administer)
moderate: Anticonvulsants (e.g., valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) - mefloquine may lower their levels and seizure control
Other antimalarials/quinine derivatives (additive cardiac and seizure risk)
minor: Live oral typhoid vaccine (complete vaccination >=3 days before first mefloquine dose)
interactions.food: Take with food and ample water to improve tolerability and absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; it may aggravate neuropsychiatric adverse effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong the QT interval on ECG.

serious: Neuropsychiatric reactions: anxiety, paranoia, depression, hallucinations, psychosis (may persist after stopping)
Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

monitoring: Neuropsychiatric status throughout therapy and follow-up
Response to malaria treatment (parasitemia, clinical improvement within 48-72 h)
ECG if used with QT-prolonging drugs or cardiac conduction defects
Liver function tests and ophthalmologic exams with prolonged prophylaxis
counsel: Stop the drug and seek care promptly for anxiety, depression, restlessness, confusion, or unusual thoughts - these can persist after stopping
Take with food and a full glass of water; for prevention take on the same day each week
Begin prophylaxis 1-2 weeks before travel and continue 4 weeks after returning
Dizziness or balance problems may occur - use caution driving or operating machinery
Tell your doctor about seizure history, psychiatric illness, or heart-rhythm problems
pk: Absorbed over hours; therapeutic blood levels within ~1 day
Plasma peak approximately 6-24 hours after a dose
Prolonged; weekly dosing maintains suppressive levels for prophylaxis
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light and moisture
pearls: BOXED-STYLE WARNING: neuropsychiatric reactions (anxiety, depression, hallucinations, psychosis) may persist for months to years after discontinuation - do not use for prophylaxis in major psychiatric disorders or seizure history
Very long half-life (~3 weeks) allows once-weekly prophylactic dosing
P. vivax needs follow-on primaquine because mefloquine does not clear hepatic hypnozoites
Do not co-administer with halofantrine (fatal QT prolongation); avoid other QT-prolonging antimalarials
If a serious neuropsychiatric symptom occurs during prophylaxis, stop and switch to an alternative
missed: For weekly prophylaxis, take the missed dose as soon as you remember, then resume the regular weekly schedule; do not take two doses close together. Do not double up.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated adverse effects including severe nausea/vomiting, dizziness, neuropsychiatric disturbances, seizures, and cardiotoxicity with QT prolongation and arrhythmias related to its quinine-like properties. Management is supportive with cardiac and neurologic monitoring; induce emesis or gastric emptying early if appropriate; treat arrhythmias and seizures. Mefloquine is not effectively removed by dialysis.
